description: Take St Paul's Cathedral apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of Wren's dome: from the ashes of the Great Fire to the tallest building in London, and the most filmed staircase in British cinema.

hotspots.text: The timber-framed outer dome, 34 meters across and rising to 85 meters, clad in lead: the great grey dome of the London skyline for 300 years.
hotspots.title: The outer dome

hotspots.text: Between the inner and outer domes hides a structural brick cone, the masonry core that actually carries the lantern, ball and cross. It is Wren's great engineering trick.
hotspots.title: The hidden brick cone

hotspots.text: About 30 meters above the floor, the circular gallery where a whisper against the wall travels clearly all the way around to the far side.
hotspots.title: The Whispering Gallery

hotspots.text: A colonnade ringing the 34 meter drum at the dome's base, making the drum read as a classical temple from the street below.
hotspots.title: The peristyle

hotspots.text: Cast in 1881 at 16 and a half tons, the largest bell in the British Isles, hung in the south-west tower.
hotspots.title: Great Paul

hotspots.text: The barrel vault over the 37 meter wide nave, rising to 27 meters. Wren designed the nave as an auditory church where the whole congregation could see and hear.
hotspots.title: The nave vault

hotspots.text: The gilded ball and cross at 111 meters, the top of the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1967.
hotspots.title: Ball and cross

intro: For 300 years the dome of St Paul's was the London skyline. Christopher Wren built it from the ashes of the Great Fire, hid a brick cone inside the dome to hold up the lantern, and gave the city a church that would star in everything from Mary Poppins to Harry Potter.
page_title: St Paul's Cathedral: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed the medieval Gothic cathedral that had stood for 400 years. Sir Christopher Wren, then 33, was given the job of replacing it, and the first stone was laid on 21 June 1675. The first service was held in 1697 with the building still unfinished, and Wren lived to see it declared complete in 1710, when the last stone of the lantern was laid by his own son. At 158 meters long and 111 meters to the top of the cross, it was the tallest building in London from 1710 until 1967, and it remains the second-largest church building in the United Kingdom by area, after Liverpool Cathedral.
sections.heading: Wren's answer to the fire

sections.body: The dome is really three domes in one. What you see from the churchyard is a timber-framed outer dome, 34 meters across and rising to 85 meters, clad in lead. Inside, 68 meters up, hangs a second, smaller painted dome, 31 meters across, the ceiling admired from the Whispering Gallery. Between them hides the structural secret: a brick cone that carries the full weight of the lantern, the gilded ball and the cross. The whole triple shell rests on eight great piers at the crossing. Around the drum runs a peristyle colonnade, a screen of columns Wren set around the dome's base that makes the drum read as a temple from the street.
sections.heading: The dome that fooled the eye

sections.body: St Paul's became the stage for the country's great farewells and celebrations. Admiral Nelson was buried in the crypt in 1806, the Duke of Wellington in 1852, and both lie there still, near Wren himself, whose plain tomb carries the famous line: reader, if you seek his monument, look around you. Winston Churchill's state funeral filled the cathedral in 1965, and in 1981 Charles and Diana were married beneath the dome. The west towers hold the bells: thirteen for change ringing in the north-west tower, and in the south-west tower Great Paul, cast in 1881 at 16 and a half tons, the largest bell in the British Isles.
sections.heading: The nation's church

sections.body:
The dome rising above the smoke of the Blitz became one of the defining images of wartime London, and filmmakers have been borrowing the building ever since. In Mary Poppins (1964) the steps and west front are the setting for "Feed the Birds," the song about the bird woman on the cathedral steps. Doctor Who has filmed at the cathedral twice: Cybermen descend the steps in the 1968 serial The Invasion and again in the 2014 story Dark Water and Death in Heaven.

The building's most-filmed interior is one most visitors never see. The Geometric Staircase in the south-west tower, Wren's self-supporting stone spiral, played the stairs to the Divination classroom in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004), appeared in The Madness of King George (1994) and in Sherlock Holmes (2009), which also used the north side of the west steps. Lawrence of Arabia (1962) shows the cathedral's exterior and the bust of T.E. Lawrence inside. In Star Trek Into Darkness (2013) the dome still stands in 23rd-century London, and in Mission: Impossible - Fallout (2018) Ethan Hunt's chase runs past St Paul's, Blackfriars Bridge and the Tate Modern.

timeline.text: The first church dedicated to St Paul is founded on Ludgate Hill.
The Great Fire of London destroys the medieval Gothic cathedral.
Wren lays the first stone of the new cathedral.
The first service is held in the unfinished building.
The cathedral is declared complete; the last stone of the lantern is laid by Wren's son.
Admiral Nelson is buried in the crypt.
Great Paul, the 16.5 ton bell, is cast for the south-west tower.
The dome stands above the smoke of the Blitz and becomes a symbol of survival.
Mary Poppins puts the cathedral steps on screen in "Feed the Birds."
Winston Churchill's state funeral is held at St Paul's.
Charles and Diana marry beneath the dome.
The Geometric Staircase plays the Divination classroom stairs in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban.
